subject: biology
topicDisplay: C1 — Interaction and interdependence: enzymes, respiration and photosynthesis
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
Random motion brings substrate and active site together
Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
Enzymes act inside cells or are secreted to act outside
Binding at an allosteric site reshapes the active site
The end product switches off the first enzyme
What cells spend ATP on
Oxidation is losing hydrogen; NAD carries it
Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
The Krebs cycle oxidizes acetyl groups and regenerates oxaloacetate
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
Light energy becomes chemical energy in carbon compounds
Oxygen is left over from splitting water
Absorption spectra and action spectra look alike but measure different things
Growing plants in extra carbon dioxide to predict the future
Photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen
Where each light-dependent reaction happens in a thylakoid
Glycerate 3-phosphate is reduced to triose phosphate
Each set of reactions depends on the other

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?
options: It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.
It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.
optionWhy: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and the enzyme is not consumed, so each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.
A student who treats the enzyme as a reactant picks this. In fact the enzyme is released unchanged when the product leaves the active site; it is not consumed.

A student who has only ever seen the catalysed reaction picks this. In fact the reaction can occur without the enzyme; the enzyme increases its rate, which at cell temperature is otherwise far too slow to sustain life.
A student who thinks enzymes 'help' by supplying energy picks this. In fact the enzyme lowers the activation energy; the energy for reaction comes from the substrate molecules' own kinetic energy.
questions.explain: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and the enzyme is not consumed, so each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.

questions.q: Which process is an example of anabolism?
options: The formation of glycogen from glucose monomers by condensation reactions
The oxidation of glucose in cell respiration to provide ATP for the cell
The digestion of starch in the gut into maltose and then glucose
The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, which releases energy
optionWhy: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

A student who classifies respiration as anabolic because it makes ATP picks this. In fact respiration oxidizes glucose to smaller molecules, so it is catabolic; ATP is the energy carrier, not a macromolecule being built.
A student who thinks digestion is anabolic because it produces useful monomers picks this. In fact digestion is hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers, a catabolic process.
A student who thinks anabolic reactions are the ones that release energy picks this. In fact anabolic reactions require energy; hydrolysis of ATP is a breaking-down reaction that releases it.
questions.explain: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

questions.q: ATP synthase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and cannot move freely. How do its substrates, ADP and phosphate, reach its active site?
options: They move by random molecular motion in the fluid and collide with the fixed active site.
They cannot, so an enzyme fixed in a membrane works only after being released from it.
The enzyme extends its active site out into the fluid to capture passing substrates.
They are carried to the enzyme by a directed flow of fluid in the mitochondrion.
optionWhy: Movement is needed for a substrate and an active site to come together, but movement of the substrate alone is enough. Enzymes immobilized in membranes are reached by substrates moving randomly.
A student who thinks both partners must move picks this. In fact substrate molecules moving randomly collide with the active site of an immobilized enzyme, which works normally.
A student who imagines enzymes reaching for substrates picks this. In fact enzymes do not seek substrates; collisions arise from random molecular motion.
A student who thinks molecules stay still unless carried picks this. In fact molecules in a fluid are in constant random motion, which alone brings them into collision with the active site.
questions.explain: Movement is needed for a substrate and an active site to come together, but movement of the substrate alone is enough. Enzymes immobilized in membranes are reached by substrates moving randomly.

questions.q: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?
options: Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.
optionWhy: At saturation the enzyme is working at its maximum rate: as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.
A student who thinks enzymes are consumed picks this. In fact enzymes are released unchanged; the plateau reflects saturation of active sites, not loss of enzyme.
A student who assumes substrate has a damaging limit like temperature picks this. In fact substrate concentration does not change the enzyme's structure.
A student who thinks enzymes supply energy picks this. In fact enzymes supply no energy; the limit is the number of active sites available for substrate to bind.
questions.explain: At saturation the enzyme is working at its maximum rate: as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.

questions.q: Which statement about intracellular and extracellular enzyme-catalysed reactions is correct?
options: Digestion in the gut is intracellular, because food is broken down inside the cells that line it.
The Krebs cycle is extracellular, because it breaks down food in the gut to release its energy.
Extracellular enzymes such as pepsin are made outside cells, which is why they act outside them.
Glycolysis is intracellular; chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.
optionWhy: A student who merges absorption with digestion picks this. In fact digestive enzymes are secreted and act in the gut lumen, outside cells; only the products are absorbed.
A student who conflates respiration with digestion picks this. In fact the Krebs cycle occurs inside cells, in mitochondria, and its substrates are products of digestion that cells have absorbed.
A student who reads 'extracellular' as describing where the enzyme is made picks this. In fact all enzymes are synthesized inside cells; extracellular enzymes are secreted to act outside.

Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle take place inside cells and are intracellular. Digestive enzymes are secreted into the gut lumen and act outside cells, so chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.
questions.explain: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle take place inside cells and are intracellular. Digestive enzymes are secreted into the gut lumen and act outside cells, so chemical digestion in the gut is extracellular.

questions.q: Which statement about non-competitive inhibition at an allosteric site is correct?
options: The inhibitor binds permanently to the allosteric site, so the enzyme is inactivated for the rest of its life.
Any molecule of a suitable size can occupy the allosteric site, and it denatures the enzyme when it does so.
The inhibitor binds reversibly away from the active site, and the resulting shape change stops catalysis.
The inhibitor occupies the active site, and adding more substrate displaces it and restores the rate.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'non-competitive' as 'irreversible' picks this. In fact binding at an allosteric site is reversible; the enzyme regains activity when the inhibitor leaves.
A student who equates inhibition with denaturation picks this. In fact only specific substances bind to an allosteric site, and the conformational change is reversible, not denaturation.

Only specific substances bind to an allosteric site. Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to conformational changes, altering the active site enough to prevent catalysis; the binding is reversible.

A student who applies the competitive mechanism to all inhibitors picks this. In fact a non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere, so extra substrate cannot displace it and the maximum rate stays lowered.
questions.explain: Only specific substances bind to an allosteric site. Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to conformational changes, altering the active site enough to prevent catalysis; the binding is reversible.

questions.q: In bacteria, threonine is converted into isoleucine by a pathway of five enzyme-catalysed steps. What happens when isoleucine is added to a growing culture?
options: Isoleucine binds to the enzyme of the final step, the one that produced it, and blocks that single step only.
Isoleucine binds to an allosteric site on the first enzyme, reversibly reducing the pathway's activity.
The five enzymes are broken down, so the pathway cannot restart after the isoleucine is used up.
Isoleucine competes with threonine for the active site of the first enzyme, blocking it competitively.
optionWhy: A student who reasons from proximity on the diagram picks this. In fact the end product inhibits the first enzyme, which stops the whole pathway and prevents intermediates from accumulating.

This is feedback inhibition: the end product, isoleucine, binds to an allosteric site on threonine deaminase, the first enzyme of the pathway. Binding is reversible, so the pathway resumes when isoleucine is used up.
A student who thinks feedback inhibition is permanent picks this. In fact the enzymes are unchanged; inhibition is released as soon as the isoleucine concentration falls.
A student who defaults to the active site for any inhibitor picks this. In fact isoleucine does not resemble threonine closely enough to compete; it binds to a separate allosteric site.
questions.explain: This is feedback inhibition: the end product, isoleucine, binds to an allosteric site on threonine deaminase, the first enzyme of the pathway. Binding is reversible, so the pathway resumes when isoleucine is used up.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a life process that ATP supplies with energy?
options: Water entering a root hair cell by osmosis uses ATP to cross the membrane against its gradient.
Joining amino acids into a polypeptide releases energy, which the cell holds as ATP.
Pumping sodium ions out of a neuron against their concentration gradient uses ATP directly.
Chromosomes move to the poles in mitosis without ATP, pulled by spindle fibres as they get shorter.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every movement across a membrane needs ATP picks this. In fact osmosis is passive: water moves down its own gradient with no ATP hydrolysed.
A student who thinks bond-forming synthesis releases energy picks this. In fact synthesis of macromolecules (anabolism) requires energy, which ATP supplies; it does not produce ATP.
Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.
A student who reads mitosis diagrams as purely mechanical picks this. In fact movement of cell components such as chromosomes is driven by motor proteins that use energy from ATP.
questions.explain: Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium-potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.

questions.q: In one reaction of the Krebs cycle, two hydrogen atoms (each with an electron) are removed from a substrate and accepted by NAD. Which statement describes this reaction?
options: The substrate is reduced and NAD is oxidized by the transfer.
Neither substance is oxidized, because no oxygen takes part in it.
The substrate is oxidized, but NAD only holds hydrogen and is unchanged.
The substrate has been oxidized and NAD has been reduced.
optionWhy: A student who attaches the labels the wrong way round picks this. In fact the substrate loses hydrogen and electrons, so it is oxidized; NAD gains them, so it is reduced.
A student who defines oxidation as gain of oxygen picks this. In fact oxidation is loss of electrons, so dehydrogenation is an oxidation whether or not oxygen is present.
A student who thinks a carrier is a passive container picks this. In fact a redox reaction always involves both changes: NAD accepts the hydrogen and is reduced to reduced NAD.

Oxidation is loss of electrons. Removing hydrogen with its electron (dehydrogenation) oxidizes the substrate, and NAD, which accepts the hydrogen, is reduced; the two occur together as a redox reaction.
questions.explain: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Removing hydrogen with its electron (dehydrogenation) oxidizes the substrate, and NAD, which accepts the hydrogen, is reduced; the two occur together as a redox reaction.

questions.q: How does anaerobic cell respiration in yeast differ from anaerobic cell respiration in human muscle?
options: Yeast uses a different pathway from glucose to pyruvate, with its own distinct set of enzymes.
Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol only, since carbon dioxide cannot form without oxygen.
There is no difference: both convert pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide when oxygen is absent.
Yeast regenerates NAD by turning pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide, not lactate.
optionWhy: A student who infers different pathways from different products picks this. In fact glycolysis is identical in yeast and humans; only the NAD-regenerating step differs.
A student who thinks carbon dioxide needs oxygen picks this. In fact yeast decarboxylates pyruvate, releasing carbon dioxide, before reducing the product to ethanol.
A student who applies the yeast equation to humans picks this. In fact human muscle reduces pyruvate directly to lactate, with no carbon dioxide released.

The pathways are the same as far as pyruvate. Yeast regenerates NAD by decarboxylating pyruvate and reducing the product to ethanol, so the final products are ethanol and carbon dioxide rather than lactate.
questions.explain: The pathways are the same as far as pyruvate. Yeast regenerates NAD by decarboxylating pyruvate and reducing the product to ethanol, so the final products are ethanol and carbon dioxide rather than lactate.

questions.q: Which statement about the Krebs cycle is correct?
options: Oxaloacetate is used up in each turn of the cycle, so it must be supplied continually from pyruvate.
Most of the ATP from aerobic respiration is formed directly by the reactions of the cycle itself.
Citrate (6C) forms when an acetyl group (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C), which is then regenerated.
Carbon dioxide is released when oxygen combines with the carbon atoms of citrate.
optionWhy: A student who expects every reactant to be consumed, as in a linear pathway, picks this. In fact oxaloacetate is regenerated by the reactions of the cycle.
A student who sees the cycle as the main energy-releasing stage picks this. In fact the cycle forms only one ATP per turn; most ATP is made by chemiosmosis using the reduced NAD.

Citrate is produced by transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. The cycle's oxidations and decarboxylations then convert citrate back to oxaloacetate, ready for the next acetyl group.
A student who thinks oxygen is a reactant of the cycle picks this. In fact carbon dioxide is released by decarboxylation; oxygen is used only as the terminal electron acceptor.
questions.explain: Citrate is produced by transfer of the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. The cycle's oxidations and decarboxylations then convert citrate back to oxaloacetate, ready for the next acetyl group.

questions.q: How does ATP synthase couple the proton gradient to the synthesis of ATP?
options: It hydrolyses ATP to pump protons across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, building the gradient.
Water moves through it by osmosis into the matrix, and the resulting pressure change forces phosphate onto ADP.
Protons collect in the intermembrane space and phosphorylate ADP there, on the outer surface of the enzyme.
Protons flow through it down their gradient into the matrix, releasing energy that phosphorylates ADP.
optionWhy: A student who takes ATP synthase for another pump picks this. In fact ATP synthase does not pump; protons flow through it passively and it makes ATP.
A student who reads 'chemiosmosis' as osmosis of water picks this. In fact it is protons, not water, that move through ATP synthase, down their concentration gradient.
A student who places ATP synthesis where the protons accumulate picks this. In fact protons pass through the enzyme into the matrix, and ADP is phosphorylated on the matrix side.
ATP synthase is the route by which protons diffuse back into the matrix. The energy released as they move down the gradient is coupled to joining phosphate to ADP: this is chemiosmosis.
questions.explain: ATP synthase is the route by which protons diffuse back into the matrix. The energy released as they move down the gradient is coupled to joining phosphate to ADP: this is chemiosmosis.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the energy transformation that takes place in photosynthesis?
options: Light energy absorbed by pigments is transformed into chemical energy in the carbon compounds made.
Energy is generated inside the chloroplast and then stored in glucose for the plant to use.
Light energy is converted into heat, which then speeds up the reactions that make glucose.
Chemical energy absorbed from the soil by the roots is transferred into the glucose molecules the leaf makes.
optionWhy: Photosynthesis is an energy transformation: light energy is absorbed by pigments and ends up as chemical energy in the bonds of carbon compounds such as glucose. This transformation supplies most of the chemical energy needed for life processes in ecosystems.
A student who thinks plants 'make energy' picks this. In fact no energy is generated: the chloroplast transforms light energy that already exists into chemical energy.

A student who can only picture light being used as heat picks this. In fact absorbed light excites electrons in pigment molecules, and the energy of those electrons is transformed into chemical energy.
A student who thinks plants obtain their food from the soil picks this. In fact the soil supplies only water and mineral ions; the energy in glucose comes from light.
questions.explain: Photosynthesis is an energy transformation: light energy is absorbed by pigments and ends up as chemical energy in the bonds of carbon compounds such as glucose. This transformation supplies most of the chemical energy needed for life processes in ecosystems.

questions.q: Which list includes all of the groups of organisms that release oxygen as a by-product of photosynthesis?
options: Plants, algae, cyanobacteria, fungi
Plants, algae and cyanobacteria
Plants and algae, no bacteria
Land plants and no other group
optionWhy: A student who thinks of fungi as plants picks this. Fungi have no photosynthetic pigments and obtain carbon compounds by absorbing them; they release no oxygen.
Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis in plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, but they split water in the same way and release oxygen.
A student who has only met bacteria as decomposers or pathogens picks this. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria that split water and release oxygen.

A student who associates photosynthesis only with green plants picks this. Algae and cyanobacteria also photosynthesize and release oxygen; most of the oxygen in the atmosphere first came from cyanobacteria.
questions.explain: Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis in plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, but they split water in the same way and release oxygen.

questions.q: Samples of an aquatic plant were exposed to light of different wavelengths and the oxygen produced was collected: at 450 nm, 12 cm³ in 10 minutes; at 550 nm, 6 cm³ in 15 minutes; at 650 nm, 15 cm³ in 15 minutes; at 700 nm, 3 cm³ in 5 minutes. Which statement about the action spectrum plotted from these data is correct?
options: The highest rate is at 650 nm, because that sample produced the most oxygen.
The rate at 550 nm should be plotted as zero, because chlorophyll reflects green.
The highest rate is at 450 nm, at 1.2 cm³ of oxygen produced per minute.
The graph shows the percentage of light at each wavelength absorbed by the pigments.
optionWhy: A student who confuses amount with rate picks this. The 650 nm sample ran for 15 minutes; its rate is 15 ÷ 15 = 1.0 cm³ per minute, lower than the 1.2 cm³ per minute at 450 nm.
A student who believes green light drives no photosynthesis picks this, ignoring the data. The sample at 550 nm produced 6 cm³ in 15 minutes, a rate of 0.4 cm³ per minute, which is low but not zero.

Rates are amounts divided by times: 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 cm³ per minute at 450 nm, 6 ÷ 15 = 0.4 at 550 nm, 15 ÷ 15 = 1.0 at 650 nm and 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6 at 700 nm. The action spectrum plots these rates against wavelength, with the peak at 450 nm.
A student who confuses the two spectra picks this. Percentage absorption is an absorption spectrum; these data give rates of photosynthesis, which plotted against wavelength make an action spectrum.
questions.explain: Rates are amounts divided by times: 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 cm³ per minute at 450 nm, 6 ÷ 15 = 0.4 at 550 nm, 15 ÷ 15 = 1.0 at 650 nm and 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6 at 700 nm. The action spectrum plots these rates against wavelength, with the peak at 450 nm.

questions.q: Tomato plants were grown in two enclosed greenhouses, one at 400 ppm carbon dioxide and one at 800 ppm. Both were kept at 22 °C with the same lighting and watering, and after six weeks the dry mass of the plants was measured. Which is a controlled variable in this experiment?
options: The carbon dioxide concentration in the greenhouses
The dry mass of the plants measured at six weeks
The plants grown at 400 ppm carbon dioxide
The temperature of 22 °C in both greenhouses
optionWhy: A student who thinks the controlled variable is the one the experimenter sets picks this. Carbon dioxide concentration is deliberately varied between the greenhouses, so it is the independent variable.

A student who thinks 'controlled' means 'carefully measured' picks this. Dry mass is what is measured to find the effect of the carbon dioxide, so it is the dependent variable; controlled variables are those held constant.

A student who merges 'control' with 'controlled variable' picks this. The plants at 400 ppm are the control treatment for comparison; a controlled variable is a factor held constant, such as temperature.

Temperature could affect growth, so it is kept the same in both greenhouses to ensure that any difference in dry mass is due to carbon dioxide alone. That makes it a controlled variable; lighting and watering are also controlled.
questions.explain: Temperature could affect growth, so it is kept the same in both greenhouses to ensure that any difference in dry mass is due to carbon dioxide alone. That makes it a controlled variable; lighting and watering are also controlled.

questions.q: Which statement about the photolysis of water in photosystem II is correct?
options: Its electrons replace those lost by the reaction centre, its protons join the gradient and oxygen is waste.
Light absorbed directly by water molecules in the thylakoid lumen breaks them apart into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
The hydrogen released from water is passed straight to NADP at photosystem II, reducing it before the electrons move on.
Oxygen is the useful product of photolysis, and the protons and electrons are waste that diffuses out of the chloroplast.
optionWhy: Photolysis in photosystem II yields electrons, which replace those emitted by the reaction-centre chlorophyll, and protons, which are released into the thylakoid lumen and add to the proton gradient. The oxygen is a waste product that diffuses away.

A student who takes 'photolysis' literally picks this. Light does not split water; the oxidized reaction centre of photosystem II pulls electrons from water, and the hydrogen is released as protons, not as hydrogen gas.

A student who links the water-splitting site directly to NADP picks this. The electrons from water pass along the chain of carriers and through photosystem I before NADP is reduced on the stroma side.
A student who sees oxygen as the point of photosynthesis picks this. It is the reverse: the protons and electrons are used in the light-dependent reactions, and oxygen is the waste product.
questions.explain: Photolysis in photosystem II yields electrons, which replace those emitted by the reaction-centre chlorophyll, and protons, which are released into the thylakoid lumen and add to the proton gradient. The oxygen is a waste product that diffuses away.

questions.q: Which statement correctly locates the light-dependent reactions within a thylakoid?
options: Water is split in the stroma, and ATP and reduced NADP are made in the thylakoid lumen, where the enzymes of the Calvin cycle then use them.
Protons are pumped out into the stroma, and ATP synthase makes ATP inside the thylakoid lumen as the protons flow back in across the membrane.
The photosystems float freely in the thylakoid lumen, and ATP synthase is embedded in the outer membrane of the chloroplast.
Water is split on the lumen side of photosystem II, ATP synthase releases ATP into the stroma and NADP is reduced on the stroma side.
optionWhy: A student who has swapped the compartments picks this. Photolysis is in the thylakoid membrane on the lumen side, ATP and reduced NADP are released into the stroma, and the Calvin cycle runs in the stroma.
A student who applies the mitochondrial arrangement the wrong way round picks this. In the chloroplast protons are pumped into the lumen and flow out to the stroma, where ATP is released.
A student who pictures photosystems as soluble picks this. Photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase are all embedded in the thylakoid membrane; none is in the chloroplast envelope.

Photolysis takes place at photosystem II on the lumen side of the thylakoid membrane, releasing protons into the lumen; ATP synthase spans the membrane and releases ATP into the stroma as protons flow out; NADP is reduced on the stroma side of photosystem I.
questions.explain: Photolysis takes place at photosystem II on the lumen side of the thylakoid membrane, releasing protons into the lumen; ATP synthase spans the membrane and releases ATP into the stroma as protons flow out; NADP is reduced on the stroma side of photosystem I.

questions.q: What is required to convert glycerate 3-phosphate into triose phosphate in the Calvin cycle?
options: ATP only; the reduced NADP is saved for the later regeneration of RuBP from triose phosphate.
Reduced NADP only; ATP from the light-dependent reactions is not used in the light-independent reactions.
ATP, which phosphorylates glycerate 3-phosphate, and reduced NADP, which reduces it.
A second molecule of carbon dioxide, which Rubisco attaches to glycerate 3-phosphate.
optionWhy: A student who has paired the two products with the wrong steps picks this. Reducing glycerate 3-phosphate needs reduced NADP as well as ATP; regenerating RuBP uses ATP only.
A student who thinks reduced NADP supplies all the energy for the Calvin cycle picks this. ATP is used both to convert glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate and to regenerate RuBP.

Glycerate 3-phosphate is converted into triose phosphate using both products of the light-dependent reactions: ATP supplies energy and a phosphate group, and reduced NADP supplies the hydrogen for the reduction.

A student who expects the carbon chain to grow at each step picks this. Both compounds have three carbons; the conversion is a reduction, and carbon dioxide is added only once per turn, by Rubisco to RuBP.
questions.explain: Glycerate 3-phosphate is converted into triose phosphate using both products of the light-dependent reactions: ATP supplies energy and a phosphate group, and reduced NADP supplies the hydrogen for the reduction.

questions.q: Algae photosynthesizing steadily in light with a plentiful supply of carbon dioxide are suddenly placed in darkness. Within a minute the concentration of glycerate 3-phosphate in the cells rises sharply. Which explanation is correct?
options: The light-independent reactions actually run faster in darkness, so glycerate 3-phosphate is produced much more quickly than it can be used up.
Reduced NADP is diverted to the chain of electron carriers to make ATP, so none of it remains to reduce glycerate 3-phosphate.
No ATP or reduced NADP is being made, so glycerate 3-phosphate cannot be reduced, while Rubisco continues to fix carbon dioxide for a time.
Glycerate 3-phosphate is no longer converted into RuBP, because the regeneration of RuBP requires light directly.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the 'dark reactions' happen in the dark picks this. The light-independent reactions slow and stop in darkness because their supply of ATP and reduced NADP has ceased.
A student who thinks reduced NADP feeds the chain picks this. Reduced NADP never donates electrons to the chloroplast chain; in the dark it is simply no longer produced.

A lack of light stops the light-dependent reactions at once. Rubisco keeps forming glycerate 3-phosphate from the remaining RuBP, but without ATP and reduced NADP it cannot be reduced to triose phosphate, so it accumulates.

A student who places the branch point of the cycle at glycerate 3-phosphate picks this. RuBP is regenerated from triose phosphate, and the block in darkness is at the reduction of glycerate 3-phosphate, which needs ATP and reduced NADP.
questions.explain: A lack of light stops the light-dependent reactions at once. Rubisco keeps forming glycerate 3-phosphate from the remaining RuBP, but without ATP and reduced NADP it cannot be reduced to triose phosphate, so it accumulates.
